steps.say: Craniosynostosis means one or more cranial sutures are fusing prematurely while the brain is still growing. The bank figure is comparing the normal skull with scaphocephaly from a fused sagittal suture, alongside a 3D CT reconstruction showing the ridged midline closure. Growth halts across the fused suture, so the vault is elongating parallel to it and producing the long narrow head.
steps.tx: **Craniosynostosis** means premature **fusion** of one or more cranial **sutures** before brain growth finishes. Growth stops across the **fused suture** while the brain keeps expanding, forcing **compensatory growth** parallel to it. The **sagittal suture** runs along the midline vault, and its early closure elongates the head into **scaphocephaly**. **3D CT reconstruction** confirms the ridged closed suture.

vis.alt: Superior view of the infant skull showing the midline sagittal suture beside scaphocephaly with a fused ridged suture and a CT reconstruction.
vis.caption: Normal skull versus scaphocephaly with 3D CT confirmation. Shapes and timing are in the text, not on the drawing (StewardMD).

steps.say: Virchow law states growth stops perpendicular to the fused suture while the open sutures are overgrowing in compensation. Fusing the midline sagittal suture prevents widening, so the head keeps growing long and narrow instead. The resulting shape is always pointing back to the suture that closed early.
steps.tx: **Virchow law** predicts the deformity: growth is **restricted** perpendicular to the **fused suture** while open sutures keep growing in **compensation**. Fuse the midline **sagittal suture** and the vault cannot widen, so it grows long and narrow. Students match each **head shape** back to the suture that closed early, applying the law across cases.

rows: Cannot widen, grows long and narrow
One forehead flattens, other side bosses

steps.say: Sagittal synostosis is the commonest single-suture form, causing over fifty percent of cases with a boat-shaped scaphocephalic head. The vault elongates with frontal bossing at one end and occipital bossing at the other, joined by a palpable midline ridge. The cephalic index falls below normal as the growing brain declares the long narrow shape in infancy.
steps.tx: **Sagittal synostosis** is the commonest single-suture form, causing over **50%** of cases with a boat-shaped **scaphocephalic** head with **dolichocephaly**. The vault elongates with **frontal bossing** at one end and **occipital bossing** at the other, joined by a palpable midline **suture ridge**. The **cephalic index** falls below normal as the long narrow shape declares itself in infancy.

rows: Ridged midline suture with bossing at both ends

steps.say: Coronal synostosis on one side gives anterior plagiocephaly with a flattened ipsilateral forehead and a bossed opposite side. The orbit is pulled upward on the fused side, producing the harlequin eye deformity seen on skull radiographs. Bilateral coronal fusion instead gives a short wide brachycephalic head while remaining symmetric.
steps.tx: Unilateral **coronal synostosis** flattens the ipsilateral forehead while the opposite side **bosses** forward, giving anterior **plagiocephaly**. Upward pull on the orbit produces the **harlequin eye** deformity seen on skull radiographs. Bilateral **coronal fusion** instead gives a short wide **brachycephalic** head without asymmetry.

rows: Anterior plagiocephaly with one flat forehead

steps.say: Metopic synostosis is closing the forehead suture early and ridging it into the triangular keel of trigonocephaly. The forehead narrows to a pointed wedge with closely set eyes, separating true fusion from a benign metopic ridge. True trigonocephaly needs vault remodelling, while a simple ridge needs only reassurance.
steps.tx: **Metopic synostosis** closes the forehead suture early and ridges it into the triangular keel of **trigonocephaly**. The forehead narrows to a pointed wedge with **hypotelorism**, separating true fusion from a benign **metopic ridge** that keeps a normal forehead shape. True **trigonocephaly** needs vault remodelling, while a simple ridge needs only reassurance.

steps.say: Crouzon syndrome is an autosomal dominant FGFR2 disorder pairing craniosynostosis with midface hypoplasia but normal hands and feet. Shallow orbits are pushing the globes forward into exorbitism, with a beaked nose and a retruded midface mimicking mandibular prognathism. Normal limbs are separating Crouzon from Apert and Pfeiffer at the bedside.
steps.tx: **Crouzon syndrome** is an autosomal dominant **FGFR2** disorder pairing craniosynostosis with **midface hypoplasia** but normal hands and feet. Shallow orbits push the globes forward into **exorbitism** with **proptosis**, with a **beaked nose** and a retruded midface mimicking **mandibular prognathism**. Normal limbs separate **Crouzon** from Apert and Pfeiffer at the bedside.

rows: Midface hypoplasia with exorbitism and beaked nose
Normal hands and feet unlike Apert and Pfeiffer

steps.say: Apert syndrome carries FGFR2 mutations at two fifty two or two fifty three, pairing bicoronal synostosis with the mitten hand of complex syndactyly. The bank figure is showing the tall skull with midface hypoplasia beside the hand with fused digits forming a single mitten. The severe hand deformity distinguishes Apert from Crouzon instantly.
steps.tx: **Apert syndrome** carries **FGFR2** mutations **Ser252Trp** or **Pro253Arg**, pairing bicoronal synostosis with severe mitten-hand **syndactyly**. The skull shows **turribrachycephaly** with **midface hypoplasia** while the digits fuse into a single mitten through complex **osseous syndactyly**. The hand deformity distinguishes **Apert** from Crouzon instantly.

vis.alt: Apert skull with turribrachycephaly and midface hypoplasia beside the mitten hand with fused digits and complex osseous syndactyly.
vis.caption: Apert skull and mitten hand. Mutation codons and timing are in the text, not on the drawing (StewardMD).

steps.say: Pfeiffer syndrome arises from FGFR1 or FGFR2 mutations, combining craniosynostosis with broad thumbs and broad great toes. The table is contrasting the three syndromes, with normal limbs pointing to Crouzon, mitten hands pointing to Apert, and broad thumbs with broad halluces pointing to Pfeiffer. Surgeons are operating between three and nine months, choosing open vault remodelling or endoscopic release with helmet therapy by age.
steps.tx: **Pfeiffer syndrome** arises from **FGFR1** or **FGFR2** mutations, combining craniosynostosis with broad **thumbs** and broad great **toes**. Wide deviated thumbs and halluces mark **Pfeiffer** against the mitten hand of Apert. Surgeons operate between **3 to 9 months**, choosing open **cranial vault remodeling** or **endoscopic suturectomy** with **helmet therapy** by age and suture count, relieving raised **intracranial pressure**.

rows: FGFR2 with normal hands and feet
FGFR2 Ser252Trp or Pro253Arg with mitten-hand syndactyly
FGFR1 or FGFR2 with broad thumbs and great toes
